composition_risks.title: Public Registry Name Collision with Internal Packages
composition_risks.description: Internal package names used within an organization are registered on public registries (npm, PyPI, Maven Central) by attackers. When build systems check both internal and public registries, the higher version number on the public registry causes the package manager to prefer the malicious public package over the legitimate internal one. This is the most common dependency confusion vector.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker discovers internal package names through leaked lock files, source code, job postings, or error messages. Attacker publishes identically-named packages on public registries with inflated version numbers (e.g., 99.0.0). Package managers configured to check multiple registries select the highest version, installing the attacker's package.
detection_methods: Monitor public registries for packages matching internal package names
Alert on dependency resolution changes in lock file diffs
Network monitoring for unexpected outbound connections during builds
Package provenance verification in CI/CD pipelines
prevention_measures: Use scoped packages (@org/package-name) on npm to prevent name collision
Configure package managers to use private registry exclusively for internal namespaces
Pin dependencies with integrity hashes in lock files
Register internal package names on public registries as placeholders
Use repository manager (Nexus, Artifactory) with routing rules
real_world_examples: Alex Birsan research (2021) affected Apple, Microsoft, PayPal via npm/PyPI/RubyGems
Researcher demonstrated attacks against 35+ organizations
Multiple follow-on attacks discovered in 2022-2024 targeting enterprise build systems
composition_risks.keywords: dependency confusion,name collision,internal packages,version resolution,registry routing

composition_risks.title: Extra Index URL Exploitation in Python pip
composition_risks.description: Python's pip tool supports multiple package indices via --extra-index-url. When configured with both a private index and PyPI, pip resolves packages from all indices and selects the highest version from any source. Attackers exploit this by publishing packages with the same names as private packages to PyPI with artificially high version numbers.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker identifies internal Python package names from leaked requirements.txt, Pipfile, or CI/CD configurations. Attacker publishes matching packages to PyPI with setup.py containing malicious code. When pip resolves dependencies from both private index and PyPI (via --extra-index-url), it prefers the higher version from PyPI, executing the attacker's setup.py during installation.
detection_methods: Audit pip configuration files for --extra-index-url usage
Monitor PyPI for packages matching internal package names using APIs
Use pip install --require-hashes to enforce expected packages
Implement dependency resolution logging in CI/CD
prevention_measures: Use --index-url (not --extra-index-url) pointing to a private repository that proxies PyPI
Configure devpi or Artifactory as the sole package index
Use pip install --require-hashes to enforce expected package hashes
Register placeholder packages on PyPI for internal package names
real_world_examples: Alex Birsan's original research specifically exploited --extra-index-url
Multiple enterprise Python build systems found vulnerable in 2021-2022
CISA advisory on dependency confusion in federal agency build systems

composition_risks.title: Maven Repository Priority Misconfiguration
composition_risks.description: Java projects using Maven may have misconfigured repository settings that cause Maven to check Maven Central before the organization's private Nexus or Artifactory instance. If internal group IDs and artifact IDs are not reserved on Maven Central, attackers can publish malicious artifacts that Maven downloads and uses in the build, potentially executing code through build plugins or lifecycle hooks.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker identifies internal Maven coordinates (group ID + artifact ID) from leaked pom.xml files, build scripts, or developer documentation. Attacker publishes artifacts with matching coordinates to Maven Central. If the organization's settings.xml lists Maven Central before the private repository, or if the artifact is not found in the private repository, Maven resolves from Maven Central.
detection_methods: Audit settings.xml and pom.xml for repository ordering
Monitor Maven Central for artifacts matching internal group IDs
Verify artifact checksums and signatures in CI/CD builds
Use Nexus/Artifactory audit logs to track dependency resolution sources
prevention_measures: Reserve internal group IDs on Maven Central
Configure Nexus/Artifactory virtual repositories with proper routing
Use Maven repository content filtering to restrict allowed remote repositories
Implement Gradle's repository content filtering for specific group IDs
Use Maven Enforcer plugin to validate dependency sources
real_world_examples: Researchers demonstrated Maven dependency confusion against Fortune 500 companies
Internal Maven group IDs found to be unreserved on Maven Central for major enterprises
Gradle builds found vulnerable due to repository ordering in settings.gradle

composition_risks.title: npm Scope Squatting and Scope Confusion
composition_risks.description: Organizations using scoped npm packages (@org/package) may be vulnerable if the scope name is not registered on the public npm registry, allowing attackers to register it. Additionally, confusion between scoped and unscoped package references in different configuration files can lead to installation of attacker-controlled packages from the public registry.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker registers a scope on npm that matches or closely resembles an organization's internal scope name. Alternatively, the attacker publishes an unscoped package with the same name as a scoped internal package (e.g., 'my-utils' vs '@company/my-utils'). Build configurations that inconsistently reference packages with and without scopes may resolve the unscoped variant from the public registry.
detection_methods: Verify all organization scope names are registered on npm
Audit package.json and lock files for inconsistent scope usage
Monitor for new npm scopes with names similar to internal scopes
Check .npmrc configuration across all projects for consistent registry routing
prevention_measures: Register organization scope on npm.js even if publishing internally
Consistently use scoped references in all package.json files
Configure .npmrc to route scoped packages to the private registry
Implement automated checks for scope consistency in CI/CD
real_world_examples: Multiple organizations found with unregistered npm scope names in 2022
Researchers demonstrated scope squatting affecting enterprise build systems
npm implemented scope reservation as a response to these attacks

composition_risks.title: Go Module Vanity Import Path Hijacking
composition_risks.description: Go modules that use vanity import paths (e.g., company.com/module instead of github.com/company/module) create a dependency on the vanity path DNS resolution. If the domain serving the vanity import path is compromised, expires, or is misconfigured, attackers can redirect module resolution to a malicious repository containing a backdoored version of the module.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker acquires the domain used for vanity import paths (through expiration, compromise, or similar domain registration). Attacker sets up a Go module vanity path server that redirects module resolution to an attacker-controlled repository. When GONOSUMDB is configured for the vanity domain (common for private modules), the module bypasses the Go checksum database, allowing the attacker's module to be used without integrity verification.
detection_methods: Monitor domain expiration for domains used in vanity import paths
Verify go.sum hashes in CI/CD pipelines
Audit GONOSUMDB and GONOSUMCHECK configurations
Monitor module proxy access logs for unexpected module sources
prevention_measures: Use github.com paths instead of vanity imports where possible
Monitor domain registration and renewal for vanity import domains
Minimize GONOSUMDB usage to only truly private modules
Use GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor for hermetic builds with vendored dependencies
Configure private Go module proxy (Athens) for internal modules
real_world_examples: Research demonstrated vanity import path hijacking through expired domains
Go module supply chain attacks documented targeting private module configurations
Expired company domains used for Go imports found available for purchase

composition_risks.title: Character Substitution in Package Names
composition_risks.description: Attackers register package names that differ from popular packages by one or two characters, exploiting common typing mistakes. Substitutions include replacing 'l' with '1', 'o' with '0', 'rn' with 'm', or doubling/omitting characters. The malicious packages contain the legitimate functionality (often by depending on the real package) plus additional malicious code for credential theft, data exfiltration, or crypto mining.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker identifies popular packages with high download counts. Attacker generates permutations of the package name using common keyboard errors, visual confusions, and character substitutions. Attacker publishes packages under these permuted names with convincing README files and descriptions. Setup scripts (setup.py, postinstall) execute malicious code upon installation. Legitimate functionality is preserved by proxying to the real package.
detection_methods: Levenshtein distance analysis of new dependencies against known-good packages
Registry-level typosquatting detection (npm and PyPI have deployed automated detection)
Pre-commit hooks validating package names against approved lists
Behavioral analysis of newly published packages for malicious patterns
prevention_measures: Always copy-paste package names from official documentation
Use lock files with integrity verification (npm ci, pip --require-hashes)
Implement package approval workflows for new dependencies in enterprise
Use tools like Socket.dev that detect typosquatting attempts
real_world_examples: crossenv (typosquat of cross-env) on npm stole environment variables
colourama (typosquat of colorama) on PyPI contained credential stealing code
Over 200 typosquatting packages discovered on npm in a single 2022 campaign

composition_risks.title: Separator and Prefix Confusion
composition_risks.description: Attackers exploit ambiguity around separators (hyphens vs underscores vs dots) and common prefixes/suffixes (python-, -js, -cli, -utils) in package names. Since package managers may normalize separators differently, a package registered with underscores might collide with one using hyphens. Additionally, adding or removing common prefixes/suffixes creates plausible alternative names.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker identifies popular packages and creates variants with different separators (python-dateutil vs python_dateutil) or with added/removed common suffixes (requests vs requests-api, lodash vs lodash-es-utils). Package managers may or may not normalize these differences. Developers searching for packages may find the attacker's variant and install it without realizing it differs from the legitimate package.
detection_methods: Normalize package names before comparison (convert all separators to a canonical form)
Cross-reference package names against official ecosystem package lists
Automated CI/CD checks that compare dependency names against normalized known-good lists
Monitor for packages with names that are separator-variants of popular packages
prevention_measures: Use the exact canonical name from the package's official documentation
Implement package name normalization in dependency management tools
Use lock files that record the resolved canonical package name
Deploy automated dependency review tools that catch separator variants
real_world_examples: PEP 503 normalization discrepancies in PyPI led to confusion attacks
npm packages with hyphen vs underscore variants used in typosquatting campaigns
NuGet packages with dot-separated names exploiting prefix confusion

composition_risks.title: Brand Impersonation Packages
composition_risks.description: Attackers publish packages using the names of well-known organizations or projects (e.g., 'azure-sdk-helper', 'google-cloud-auth', 'aws-cdk-tools') to appear official. These packages use convincing descriptions, README files, and even AI-generated documentation to appear legitimate. Brand impersonation is increasingly automated, with attackers publishing hundreds of impersonation packages simultaneously.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker identifies popular cloud providers, frameworks, or organizations and generates plausible package names using their branding. Attacker creates packages with professional-looking README files (often AI-generated), fake contributor profiles, and descriptions that reference legitimate documentation. Developers searching for official packages may find and install the impersonation package, which executes malicious payloads targeting cloud credentials and API keys.
detection_methods: Verify package publisher identity against the claimed organization
Check package age, download count, and community engagement metrics
Cross-reference packages against official SDK documentation from the vendor
Use registry-provided verified publisher badges (npm, PyPI)
prevention_measures: Only install packages from official documentation links, never from search results alone
Verify publisher identity on the registry (npm verified publishers, PyPI trusted publishers)
Use organization-curated registries that vet packages before inclusion
Train developers to verify package authenticity before installation
real_world_examples: 2023: hundreds of npm/PyPI packages impersonating Azure, GCP, and AWS discovered
AI-generated README files making impersonation packages appear more legitimate
Impersonation packages targeting cloud credentials found exfiltrating to Telegram

composition_risks.title: Star-Jacking: Fake Popularity Signals
composition_risks.description: Attackers create packages on registries and associate them with popular GitHub repositories they do not own, inheriting the star count and social proof of the legitimate project. This makes the malicious package appear popular and trustworthy to developers who assess packages based on GitHub stars. Some registries display linked repository statistics on the package page without verifying ownership.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker creates a new package on a registry (npm, PyPI, Go). Attacker sets the package's repository URL or homepage to point to a popular, unrelated GitHub repository. The registry displays the linked repository's star count, contributor count, and activity metrics alongside the malicious package. Developers see the high star count and mistakenly trust the package.
detection_methods: Verify that the package's repository URL matches the actual source code of the package
Compare the package name with the repository name for consistency
Check that the package author matches the repository owner
Use tools that verify repository-to-package linkage
prevention_measures: Verify package source by checking the actual repository contents, not just the star count
Use npm provenance or PyPI attestations to verify the source repository link
Check if the package is listed in the linked repository's documentation
Report star-jacked packages to the registry for removal
real_world_examples: Go packages found star-jacking popular repositories to inflate credibility
npm packages linking to unrelated high-star repos to appear legitimate
Researchers identified hundreds of star-jacked packages across ecosystems in 2023

composition_risks.title: Combosquatting: Legitimate Name Plus Extra Word
composition_risks.description: Attackers register package names that combine a legitimate popular package name with an additional word, creating a plausible-sounding package name (e.g., 'react-native-util' when the real package is 'react-native-utils', or 'lodash-helpers' as a supposed extension to lodash). These names are designed to appear as official extensions, utilities, or helpers for the legitimate package.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker identifies popular packages and creates variants by adding common suffixes like -utils, -helpers, -core, -cli, -tools, -sdk, -api, -client, -server. The resulting names sound like official extensions or related tools. Developers searching for functionality related to the popular package may discover and install the combosquatted package instead of finding the legitimate utility.
detection_methods: Fuzzy string matching of new packages against popular package names
Monitor for packages that reference popular packages in their name but come from unrelated authors
Automated analysis of dependency additions for combosquatting patterns
Community reporting of suspicious package names
prevention_measures: Search for packages through official documentation and verified sources
Verify that package authors are associated with the claimed parent project
Use dependency approval workflows that require review of new packages
Configure SCA tools to flag combosquatting attempts
real_world_examples: Multiple npm packages using react-native-* prefix for malicious packages
PyPI packages combining popular names with -sdk, -api suffixes
Maven packages using popular group IDs with additional artifact words

composition_risks.title: Account Takeover via Credential Stuffing
composition_risks.description: Attackers use leaked credential databases from other breaches to attempt login to package registry accounts. If a maintainer reused their password across services, the attacker gains access to their registry account and can publish malicious versions of any package they maintain. This is the most common vector for maintainer account compromise due to the widespread problem of password reuse.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker obtains credential databases from past data breaches (available on dark web markets). Attacker attempts login to npm, PyPI, RubyGems, and other registries using the leaked email/password combinations. If the maintainer reused their password, the attacker gains full access to their account. Attacker publishes malicious versions of the maintainer's packages, which are automatically adopted by systems using version ranges.
detection_methods: Monitor for login attempts from unusual locations or IPs
Detect publication of new versions from unusual network contexts
Alert on rapid succession of version publications
Implement behavioral analysis of account activity patterns
prevention_measures: Require MFA for all package registry accounts
Use unique passwords for each registry account
Implement registry-side credential checking against breach databases
Use OIDC-based publishing (npm provenance, PyPI Trusted Publishers) instead of API tokens
Monitor for credential leaks using services like Have I Been Pwned
real_world_examples: ua-parser-js (2021) compromised through account takeover
eslint-scope (2018) npm account compromised via reused credentials
Multiple PyPI maintainer accounts compromised through credential stuffing in 2023

composition_risks.title: Long-Term Social Engineering for Commit Access
composition_risks.description: Sophisticated attackers invest months or years building trust with open source project maintainers before requesting and receiving commit or publish access. Once granted access, the attacker introduces subtle, hard-to-detect malicious code through carefully crafted commits that appear to be legitimate contributions. This is the most difficult supply chain attack to prevent because the attacker has legitimate access.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker creates a convincing developer persona with a history of legitimate contributions across multiple projects. Attacker targets a specific project by submitting useful bug fixes, documentation improvements, and feature additions over an extended period (months to years). Attacker may pressure the maintainer by simultaneously creating issues about responsiveness, suggesting the project needs more help. Once granted maintainer access, the attacker introduces malicious code, often hidden in build scripts, test fixtures, or obfuscated within complex code changes.
detection_methods: Behavioral analysis of contributor patterns over extended periods
Monitoring for changes to build infrastructure, test fixtures, and CI/CD configuration
Independent security review of all changes by security-focused reviewers
Reproducible builds to detect build-time code injection
prevention_measures: Require multiple independent reviewers for all changes to security-critical code
Use CODEOWNERS to enforce review requirements for build scripts and CI/CD files
Implement waiting periods before granting commit access to new contributors
Maintain bus factor greater than 1 for all critical projects
Support maintainers financially to reduce pressure to delegate
real_world_examples: xz-utils backdoor (CVE-2024-3094): attacker spent 2+ years building trust before inserting backdoor
Multiple incidents of compromised contributors in smaller npm packages
Linux kernel has caught attempted social engineering for commit access

composition_risks.title: CI/CD Token Leakage and Exploitation
composition_risks.description: Package registry authentication tokens stored in CI/CD systems are exposed through misconfigured pipeline logs, improperly scoped secrets, or CI/CD system vulnerabilities. Leaked tokens enable attackers to publish packages without compromising the maintainer's account directly. CI/CD tokens often have broad publish access and may lack the security controls (MFA, IP restrictions) applied to interactive logins.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Tokens are leaked through: verbose CI/CD logging that outputs environment variables, misconfigured GitHub Actions that expose secrets to fork PRs, compromised CI/CD pipeline steps that exfiltrate secrets, or secrets stored in public repository configuration files. Once the token is obtained, the attacker can use the npm/PyPI/RubyGems CLI to publish new versions of any package the token has access to.
detection_methods: Secret scanning in repositories and CI/CD configurations (Gitleaks, truffleHog)
Monitor package publications for unusual user agents or source IPs
Registry audit logs showing token usage from unexpected locations
Automated detection of tokens in CI/CD log output
prevention_measures: Use OIDC-based publishing instead of stored tokens (npm provenance, PyPI Trusted Publishers)
Scope tokens to specific packages and operations
Enable CI/CD secret masking for all log output
Rotate tokens regularly and audit token permissions
Use short-lived tokens generated at deployment time
real_world_examples: Thousands of npm tokens found exposed in public GitHub repositories
Codecov breach (2021) exfiltrated CI/CD environment variables including tokens
GitHub Actions secret exposure through pull_request_target misuse

composition_risks.title: Protestware and Intentional Sabotage
composition_risks.description: Legitimate maintainers intentionally introduce destructive or malicious code into their packages as a form of protest, expression, or retaliation. Unlike external attacks, protestware comes from the authorized maintainer, making it undetectable by authentication and authorization controls. Motivations include protesting unpaid open source labor, geopolitical statements, or frustration with the open source ecosystem.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Maintainer publishes a new version containing destructive code (infinite loops, file deletion, data corruption) or code targeting specific groups (geo-targeted attacks based on IP or locale). Because the maintainer has legitimate publish access, the malicious version is indistinguishable from a legitimate update. Systems using automatic updates or loose version ranges receive the sabotaged version without review.
detection_methods: Behavioral analysis detecting sudden major changes in package code
Automated detection of destructive operations (file deletion, infinite loops)
Community monitoring and rapid response for popular packages
CI/CD timeouts and resource limits to catch infinite loop scenarios
prevention_measures: Pin dependency versions in lock files and review all updates manually
Implement CI/CD timeouts to detect infinite loop sabotage
Maintain forks of critical dependencies as fallback
Support open source maintainers financially to reduce burnout and frustration
Use SCA tools that detect behavioral changes between versions
real_world_examples: colors.js (2022): maintainer added infinite loop, affected 23M weekly downloads
node-ipc (2022): maintainer added geo-targeted file overwrite for Russian/Belarusian IPs
faker.js (2022): maintainer deleted all code, replaced with empty module

composition_risks.title: Email Domain Expiration and Account Recovery Exploitation
composition_risks.description: Package registry accounts registered with email addresses on expired or available domains can be taken over by acquiring the domain and using password reset mechanisms. This attack exploits the gap between domain registration lifecycle and package registry account lifecycle. A maintainer who changes email providers or lets a domain expire may unknowingly leave their registry account recoverable by anyone who purchases the expired domain.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker identifies package maintainers whose registered email domains have expired or are available for purchase. Attacker purchases the expired domain and sets up an email server. Attacker uses the registry's password reset mechanism to send a reset link to the now-attacker-controlled email address. After resetting the password, the attacker has full access to the maintainer's account and all their published packages.
detection_methods: Monitor domain expiration dates for email domains used by package maintainers
Registry-side alerts for password resets from newly registered domains
Detect publications from accounts after extended periods of inactivity
Automated scanning of maintainer email domain availability
prevention_measures: Enable MFA on all registry accounts (prevents email-only account recovery)
Use email addresses on stable, long-term domains (e.g., @gmail.com)
Registries should implement additional verification for dormant account recovery
Monitor email domain status for maintainers of critical dependencies
real_world_examples: Academic research found significant portion of npm maintainers use expired domains
Researchers purchased expired domains and demonstrated potential account takeover for packages with millions of downloads
npm implemented additional security measures for dormant accounts as a response

composition_risks.title: Data Exfiltration via Install Scripts
composition_risks.description: Malicious packages execute code during the installation phase (npm postinstall, Python setup.py, RubyGems extconf.rb) that collects and exfiltrates sensitive data from the developer's or build system's environment. Targeted data includes environment variables, SSH keys, AWS/Azure/GCP credentials, browser cookies, cryptocurrency wallet files, and source code from the local filesystem.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker publishes a package with malicious code in install-time hooks. On npm, the postinstall script runs automatically. On PyPI, setup.py executes during pip install. The malicious code collects sensitive files and environment variables, encodes them (base64), and transmits them to attacker-controlled endpoints via HTTP requests, DNS exfiltration, or webhooks (Discord, Telegram, Slack).
detection_methods: Analyze install scripts for network requests and file system reads
Detect base64 encoding of sensitive file paths
Monitor for webhook URLs (Discord, Telegram) in package code
Network monitoring during package installation for unexpected connections
Static analysis of package code for credential access patterns
prevention_measures: Use --ignore-scripts flag for npm installations where feasible
Install packages in isolated environments (containers, VMs)
Run security scanners on new dependencies before adoption
Implement egress filtering on build systems to block unauthorized connections
Use SCA tools that analyze package behavior, not just known CVEs
real_world_examples: W4SP Stealer campaign (2022-2023): hundreds of PyPI packages exfiltrating Discord tokens and browser data
eslint-scope compromise: postinstall script exfiltrated npm tokens
Multiple npm packages found exfiltrating environment variables to Discord webhooks

composition_risks.title: Cryptocurrency Mining in Build Environments
composition_risks.description: Malicious packages include cryptocurrency mining code that activates during installation or when the package is imported. Mining code may be embedded directly in the package, downloaded at runtime from external servers, or hidden in native binary extensions. CI/CD environments are particularly targeted because they provide compute resources that are consumed and billed automatically without close monitoring.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker includes cryptocurrency mining code (typically XMRig for Monero) in a package. The miner may activate: during postinstall (npm), in setup.py (PyPI), when the package is imported at runtime, or through a native binary extension. For CI/CD targeting, the miner only activates in environments detected as CI/CD (by checking CI-specific environment variables like CI=true, GITHUB_ACTIONS=true).
detection_methods: Monitor CPU and resource usage during package installation
Detect known mining pool connections in network traffic (e.g., pool.minexmr.com)
Scan packages for cryptocurrency mining binaries or scripts
Alert on unusual compute consumption spikes in CI/CD environments
prevention_measures: Use --ignore-scripts to prevent postinstall execution
Implement CPU and memory limits on CI/CD build containers
Block known mining pool domains at the network level
Scan all new packages for binary payloads
Monitor cloud billing for unexpected compute cost increases
real_world_examples: event-stream compromise included Copay wallet-targeting cryptominer
Multiple npm packages found with XMRig miners in 2019-2023
PyPI packages containing hidden cryptocurrency mining code discovered in bulk

composition_risks.title: Backdoor Installation via Supply Chain
composition_risks.description: Sophisticated attackers use supply chain attacks to install persistent backdoors in target systems. Unlike simple data theft, backdoor-focused attacks aim to establish long-term unauthorized access that persists beyond the initial compromise. The backdoor may be injected during build, activated conditionally based on environment detection, and designed to be difficult to detect through static analysis.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker compromises a package used in the target's dependency tree (directly or transitively). The malicious code installs a persistent backdoor: reverse shell, SSH authorized key, webshell, or modified authentication mechanism. The backdoor may activate only in specific environments (production, specific hostname, IP range) to avoid detection during development and testing. Obfuscation, encryption, and multi-stage loading are used to evade static analysis.
detection_methods: Runtime behavioral monitoring for unexpected network connections
File integrity monitoring for unauthorized modifications
Endpoint detection for known backdoor patterns
Comparison of build output against expected content (reproducible builds)
Memory analysis for injected code or modified system functions
prevention_measures: Implement SLSA Level 3+ build integrity controls
Use reproducible builds to detect build-time code injection
Deploy endpoint detection and response (EDR) on all systems
Monitor for unauthorized network listeners and reverse shells
Conduct regular security assessments including runtime analysis
real_world_examples: SolarWinds SUNBURST backdoor in Orion (2020)
xz-utils backdoor targeting OpenSSH authentication (CVE-2024-3094)
3CX DesktopApp compromise distributing backdoored application update (2023)

composition_risks.title: Dependency Tree Injection via Transitive Dependencies
composition_risks.description: Attackers target less-scrutinized transitive dependencies (dependencies of dependencies) rather than high-profile direct dependencies. By compromising a deeply nested package with fewer users and less security attention, the attacker can reach high-value targets through the dependency chain. The attack is harder to detect because developers typically focus security attention on direct dependencies.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker identifies a transitive dependency used by a high-value target (e.g., a package used by a popular framework). The transitive dependency has fewer maintainers, less community oversight, and weaker security practices. Attacker compromises the transitive dependency through any vector (account takeover, social engineering, typosquatting). When the target application resolves its dependency tree, the compromised transitive dependency is included and its malicious code executes.
detection_methods: Full dependency tree analysis including all transitive dependencies
Monitor all dependencies (not just direct) for version changes and new publications
SCA tools that analyze the complete dependency graph for security issues
Alert on dependency tree changes that introduce new transitive dependencies
prevention_measures: Use lock files to pin all dependencies (including transitive) with integrity hashes
Implement SCA scanning covering the full dependency tree
Review transitive dependency changes in lock file diffs
Minimize the dependency tree by choosing dependencies with fewer sub-dependencies
Consider vendoring critical dependency trees for maximum control
real_world_examples: event-stream attack used flatmap-stream (transitive dependency) as the attack vector
Several npm supply chain attacks targeted deep transitive dependencies
Python packages found to inject malicious code via deeply nested dependencies

composition_risks.title: Conditional Payload Activation to Evade Detection
composition_risks.description: Advanced malicious packages include payloads that activate only under specific conditions, evading detection in development, testing, and scanning environments. Conditions may include: specific environment variables (production), target hostname patterns, geographic IP ranges, time-based activation (delayed execution), or detection of specific software (e.g., Copay wallet). This makes the malicious code invisible during security analysis.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Malicious code checks for activation conditions before executing: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production', hostname.includes('target-corp'), IP geolocation in target country, time-delayed activation (only after N days of installation), or presence of specific files/processes indicating the target application. Scanning tools that run in generic environments never trigger the payload, causing the package to appear clean.
detection_methods: Dynamic analysis in environments mimicking production conditions
Behavioral analysis across multiple environment configurations
Code analysis for environment-checking patterns and conditional execution
Sandboxed execution with varied environment variables and configurations
Deobfuscation and control flow analysis of suspected packages
prevention_measures: Use SCA tools that perform dynamic analysis in varied environments
Monitor production systems for unexpected behaviors from known packages
Implement runtime application self-protection (RASP)
Review package code for environment-checking logic
Deploy behavioral monitoring that detects anomalous package behavior in production
real_world_examples: event-stream activated only in Copay wallet context via environmental detection
node-ipc activated geo-targeted payload based on IP geolocation
Multiple malicious packages using process.env checks to target production environments

composition_risks.title: Unmaintained Critical Package with Known Vulnerabilities
composition_risks.description: A widely-used package is abandoned by its maintainer without designating a successor, leaving known vulnerabilities unpatched. Consumers continue using the package because migration to alternatives requires significant effort. The package accumulates known vulnerabilities that are publicly documented but never fixed, creating a persistent security risk for all dependent applications.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: This is not an active attack but a passive risk. The maintainer stops responding to issues, pull requests, and vulnerability reports. Security researchers discover vulnerabilities and file CVEs, but patches are never released. Attackers can exploit the known, unpatched vulnerabilities in any application using the abandoned package. The risk increases over time as more vulnerabilities are discovered.
detection_methods: Monitor dependency maintenance status (last commit date, issue responsiveness)
Track CVE publications for all dependencies
Use OpenSSF Scorecard to assess project health and maintenance
Alert when dependency repositories are archived or marked as deprecated
prevention_measures: Regularly audit dependency health and maintenance status
Have migration plans for critical dependencies with low bus factor
Fork and maintain critical abandoned dependencies if alternatives do not exist
Contribute to open source projects to reduce abandonment risk
Use alternative packages with larger, more active maintainer communities
real_world_examples: event-stream was essentially unmaintained when it was compromised
Numerous npm packages with millions of weekly downloads have single maintainers who have become inactive
Python packages in core scientific computing stack have experienced maintainer burnout

composition_risks.title: Abandoned Package Name Reclaim and Hijacking
composition_risks.description: When a package is abandoned and its name becomes available (through deletion, transfer, or registry name recycling policies), attackers acquire the package name and publish a new version containing malicious code. Systems configured to accept updates from the package automatically install the attacker's version, believing it to be a legitimate update from the original maintainer.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Attacker monitors package registries for abandoned packages (no updates for extended periods, maintainer inactive). Attacker requests package name transfer through the registry's transfer policies or waits for the name to be released. Once the attacker controls the package name, they publish a new version with a higher version number containing malicious code. Consumers using version ranges (^, ~, *) in their package specifications automatically receive the new malicious version.
detection_methods: Monitor package ownership changes for all dependencies
Alert on new versions of previously dormant packages
Track registry transfer requests and ownership changes via APIs
Detect sudden download count increases for previously inactive packages
prevention_measures: Pin exact dependency versions in lock files
Monitor dependency ownership changes through registry APIs
Review all dependency updates before adoption, especially for dormant packages
Subscribe to security advisories for all dependencies
Implement dependency monitoring services that track ownership changes
real_world_examples: npm packages reclaimed through name transfer policies and used for malware
PyPI packages republished by new owners with malicious code
Multiple incidents of abandoned Go modules being repurposed for attacks

composition_risks.title: Single Maintainer Risk (Bus Factor = 1)
composition_risks.description: Packages maintained by a single individual represent a critical supply chain risk. If the sole maintainer becomes unavailable (burnout, life changes, health issues, loss of interest), the package has no one to address security vulnerabilities, review contributions, or publish updates. This creates a window for social engineering attacks, as pressure to find a new maintainer may lead to granting access to unvetted individuals.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: This is a systemic risk rather than a specific attack technique. When a sole maintainer becomes unavailable: vulnerability reports go unaddressed, build infrastructure may degrade, CI/CD tokens may expire without rotation, and the package may become incompatible with updated dependencies. Attackers may target single-maintainer packages specifically because: they can social-engineer maintainer access more easily, there is no second reviewer for code changes, and the maintainer may be more susceptible to burnout-driven carelessness.
detection_methods: Assess bus factor for all dependencies using OpenSSF Scorecard
Monitor maintainer activity levels (commit frequency, issue responsiveness)
Track contributor diversity and participation trends
Alert when a critical dependency's sole maintainer becomes inactive
prevention_measures: Prioritize dependencies with diverse maintainer teams
Contribute to critical open source dependencies to increase bus factor
Support single-maintainer projects through sponsorship and contribution
Maintain internal forks or vendor critical single-maintainer dependencies
Evaluate maintainer sustainability when selecting new dependencies
real_world_examples: xz-utils had effectively a single maintainer, enabling the social engineering attack
event-stream was single-maintainer before the compromise
left-pad (2016): single maintainer unpublished a critical package, breaking thousands of builds

composition_risks.title: Deprecated Package Without Migration Path
composition_risks.description: A maintainer deprecates a package and recommends migration to an alternative, but the migration requires significant code changes that many consumers defer or never complete. The deprecated package continues to be used in production while receiving no security updates. Unlike truly abandoned packages, deprecated packages have an explicit end-of-life declaration but consumers fail to act on it.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: The deprecated package continues to run in production environments without security updates. New vulnerabilities discovered in the deprecated code are never patched. Attackers who discover or learn of vulnerabilities in the deprecated package can exploit them across all systems still using it. The deprecation itself may reduce community vigilance about the package's security.
detection_methods: Track deprecation notices from package registries (npm deprecation warnings, PyPI classifiers)
Audit dependencies for deprecated packages using SCA tools
Monitor CVE publications for deprecated packages in use
CI/CD checks that fail or warn on deprecated dependency usage
prevention_measures: Create and maintain a dependency migration backlog
Prioritize migration of deprecated dependencies in security-critical paths
Set organizational policies for maximum time to migrate from deprecated packages
Evaluate migration complexity when initially adopting dependencies
Use SCA tools that flag deprecated packages with urgency-based scoring
real_world_examples: request (npm): deprecated in 2020, still had millions of weekly downloads years later
Python 2 packages: many packages dropped Python 2 support but consumers continued using old versions
Multiple deprecated crypto libraries still in widespread use despite known weaknesses

composition_risks.title: Protestware: Politically Motivated Code Modification
composition_risks.description: A category of supply chain risk where maintainers introduce politically motivated code into their packages. Unlike sabotage for personal grievances, protestware is motivated by geopolitical events, social causes, or ideological positions. The modifications may be destructive (data deletion, service disruption), informational (displaying messages), or targeted (affecting users based on geography, language, or organizational affiliation).
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Maintainer publishes a new version containing code that evaluates the user's context (IP geolocation, system locale, timezone, hostname) and takes action based on political criteria. Actions range from displaying protest messages to deleting files or disrupting services. Because the maintainer has legitimate access, the code passes all authentication and authorization controls. Version ranges in dependency specifications cause automatic adoption.
detection_methods: Monitor package updates for geolocation checks and locale-based conditions
Behavioral analysis detecting new capabilities (network calls, file operations) in updates
Community reporting and rapid response for popular packages
Automated analysis of package updates for destructive operations
prevention_measures: Pin dependency versions and review all updates before adoption
Implement behavioral analysis for dependency updates
Maintain forks of critical dependencies as fallback
Use SCA tools that detect behavioral changes between versions
Implement geo-diverse testing to catch geo-targeted payloads
real_world_examples: node-ipc peacenotwar module (2022): geo-targeted file overwrite for Russian/Belarusian IPs
es5-ext (2022): displayed anti-war message for Russian locale systems
event-source-polyfill (2022): replaced README with anti-war statement

composition_risks.title: License Change Attack on Downstream Dependencies
composition_risks.description: A maintainer changes the license of their package to a more restrictive license (e.g., from MIT to AGPL or SSPL) without adequate notice. This can create legal compliance issues for downstream consumers who have built commercial products incorporating the package under the original permissive license. While not a traditional security attack, license changes can force emergency dependency migrations and create legal risk.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: Maintainer publishes a new version with a changed license. Consumers who automatically update receive the new license terms, which may be incompatible with their business model or compliance requirements. In some cases, the license change is retroactive or ambiguous, creating uncertainty about the license status of existing deployments. Companies may face legal risk if they continue using the package under the new terms.
detection_methods: Monitor license field changes in dependency updates
SCA tools that track license changes between versions
Automated license compliance checks in CI/CD pipelines
Legal review triggers for dependency license modifications
prevention_measures: Implement automated license compliance checking in CI/CD
Define an approved license list for the organization
Monitor license changes in dependency updates using tools like FOSSA or Snyk
Pin dependency versions and review license changes before updating
Maintain legal review process for dependency license changes
real_world_examples: Elasticsearch license change from Apache 2.0 to SSPL (2021)
MongoDB license change from AGPL to SSPL (2018)
Redis modules license change from BSD to dual license (2018)
Terraform license change from MPL to BSL (2023)

composition_risks.title: Dependency Bloat and Phantom Dependencies
composition_risks.description: Excessive dependency chains create an expanded attack surface where the application transitively depends on hundreds or thousands of packages, many of which are unnecessary or could be replaced with built-in functionality. Phantom dependencies (packages that are transitively included but never actually used by the application) increase the attack surface without providing any functional benefit. Each additional dependency is a potential supply chain attack vector.
composition_risks.attack_mechanism: This is a passive risk rather than an active attack. Each dependency in the tree represents a potential attack vector: it has maintainers who could be compromised, code that could contain vulnerabilities, and a distribution channel that could be tampered with. Applications with deep dependency trees have a much larger attack surface. Dependency bloat makes it impractical to review, audit, or monitor all dependencies, reducing the likelihood that a compromised dependency would be detected.
detection_methods: Dependency tree analysis to identify unused transitive dependencies
Dead code analysis to detect imported but unused packages
Dependency count metrics and trend monitoring
Tools like depcheck (npm) or pipdeptree (Python) to analyze dependency trees
prevention_measures: Prefer packages with fewer transitive dependencies
Regularly audit and remove unused dependencies
Use dependency analysis tools to identify unnecessary packages
Consider implementing functionality directly instead of adding small-utility packages
Evaluate the full dependency tree before adopting new dependencies
real_world_examples: left-pad incident (2016): 11-line package was a dependency of thousands of projects
is-odd, is-even, is-number: trivial npm packages with millions of downloads
Average npm project has 100+ transitive dependencies, many never used
